intro: Set a needle in the groove of a spinning record and a voice fills the room. Flip a switch and light crosses the room faster than you can blink. Tap send on a phone and a picture of Lake Michigan reaches a cousin in another state in about a second. None of these carry any stuff from one place to the other. The record stays on the turntable, the bulb stays in the ceiling, the phone stays in your hand. What travels is a pattern: a wave.

This unit is about waves and what they can carry. You will start with ripples on the wave bench and drums on the drum bench, learning to measure amplitude, wavelength and frequency. You will follow sound through air, water and steel into the ear, and light through glass and water into the eye. Then you will see how people turned those same waves into instruments: the microscope that showed Hooke his cells, the telescope that showed Galileo four moons, the radio, the fiber cable and the weather radar that warns of a tornado.

By the end you should be able to explain why sound goes silent in a vacuum while light does not, why a pencil looks bent in water, how two lenses make a microscope, why a digital photo survives a noisy connection when a record groove cannot, and how a bat, a submarine and a weather station all use the same trick of timing an echo.
bigQuestion: How do waves carry energy and information, and how have people learned to use them to see, hear and communicate beyond the reach of their own senses?

timeline.t: Galileo turns a two-lens spyglass on Jupiter and finds four moons circling it
Robert Boyle pumps the air from a jar and shows sound needs a medium
Robert Hooke publishes microscope drawings of cork and names the cell
Isaac Newton builds a telescope that gathers light with a mirror instead of a lens
Ole Roemer uses eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io to show that light has a finite speed
William Herschel finds invisible infrared light beyond the red end of a spectrum
Thomas Edison records and plays back a voice from a groove on a tinfoil cylinder
Heinrich Hertz makes and detects radio waves in his laboratory
Wilhelm Röntgen discovers X-rays and photographs the bones of a hand
The 40-inch Yerkes refractor opens in Wisconsin, the largest lens telescope ever used
The Hubble Space Telescope is launched above the blurring atmosphere
The James Webb Space Telescope launches to see the universe in infrared

words.d: a repeating disturbance that carries energy from one place to another without carrying the medium
how far the medium moves from rest; larger amplitude means more energy
the distance from one crest of a wave to the next
the number of complete waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz
the material a mechanical wave travels through, such as air, water or steel
a wave, such as sound, that needs a medium to travel
a wave of electric and magnetic fields, such as light, that needs no medium
the bending of light as it changes speed entering a new material
a curved piece of clear material that refracts light to focus or magnify it
the full range of electromagnetic waves from radio to gamma rays
a signal made of numbers stored as ones and zeros, which resists noise and copies exactly
a reflected wave whose delay tells how far away the reflecting object is

test.q: A ripple crosses a pond and passes a floating leaf. What does the leaf mainly do?
choices: Travels with the ripple to the shore
Bobs up and down and stays nearly in place
test.why: Waves carry energy, not the medium. The leaf rises and falls as the ripple passes but does not travel with it.

test.q: Which pair of changes would make a sound both louder and higher in pitch?
test.why: Loudness comes from amplitude and pitch from frequency. Louder and higher means larger amplitude and higher frequency.

test.q: A wave on the bench has frequency 3 Hz and wavelength 0.5 m. What is its speed?
test.why: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength: 3 times 0.5 is 1.5 meters per second.

test.q: Why can a bell not be heard inside a jar with the air pumped out?
choices: Sound needs a medium, and there are no particles to carry the vibration
The bell stops ringing without air
The vacuum makes the sound too fast to hear
test.why: Sound is a mechanical wave. With no particles to push, the vibration of the bell cannot reach the glass.

test.q: In which medium does sound travel fastest?
choices: Sound travels at the same speed in all three
test.why: Tightly packed, stiffly bonded particles pass pushes along quickly. Sound moves about 6,000 m/s in steel, 1,480 in water and 343 in air.

test.q: Where in the ear do vibrations become nerve signals?
test.why: Hair cells along the membrane inside the fluid-filled cochlea fire nerve signals when their part of the membrane moves.

test.q: Why can sunlight cross space to reach Earth?
choices: Space is full of thin air
The sun pushes the light with solar wind
Light is an electromagnetic wave and needs no medium
test.why: Unlike sound, light carries its own electric and magnetic fields and travels through a vacuum at about 300,000 km/s.

test.q: A red apple looks red because it:
choices: Reflects red light and absorbs most other colors
test.why: We see the light an object sends back. The apple reflects red wavelengths and absorbs most of the green and blue.

test.q: What directly causes light to bend when it enters water from air?
choices: Light changes speed at the surface
Light changes color at the surface
test.why: Light slows down in water. At an angle, the change in speed swings the beam, which is refraction.

test.q: A student sees distant signs as a blur but reads a book easily. Which lens fixes this?
choices: A convex lens, thicker in the middle
A concave lens, thinner in the middle
test.why: She is nearsighted: light focuses in front of the retina. A concave lens spreads the rays so the focus lands on the retina.

test.q: A microscope with a 10x objective and a 20x eyepiece magnifies:
test.why: The eyepiece magnifies the image the objective already made, so the two multiply: 10 times 20 is 200.

test.q: Why are the biggest telescopes built with mirrors rather than lenses?
choices: A mirror can be supported from behind and made very large without sagging
Mirrors do not need to be pointed at the sky
test.why: A lens is held only at its edge and bends under its own weight past about a meter. A mirror can be huge.

test.q: Which electromagnetic wave has the highest frequency and the most energy per wave?
test.why: Shorter wavelength means higher frequency and more energy. X-rays are far shorter than visible, infrared or radio waves.

test.q: Why does a digital copy of a song stay perfect while an analog tape copy gains hiss?
choices: Digital signals travel by light only
Digital bits are read as ones and zeros, so small noise is discarded instead of copied
test.why: Noise added to an analog shape becomes part of the shape. Noise added to a bit is ignored as long as high and low can still be told apart.

test.q: A sonar ping in seawater, about 1,500 m/s, returns after 4 seconds. How deep is the bottom?
test.why: The round trip is 1,500 times 4, or 6,000 meters. The sound went down and back, so the depth is half: 3,000 meters.

write.prompt: Make a claim: Is a digital signal or an analog signal the better way to store and send a recording of a song? Support it with evidence from this unit about waves, noise, copying and the way a phone sends a picture, and explain your reasoning.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence at the start.
Use at least two pieces of evidence: how noise affects a record groove or tape, how bits survive a noisy connection, and how sample rate limits what a digital file keeps.
Explain the reasoning: say why each piece of evidence supports your claim, using the words amplitude, noise and bit.
Give the other side a fair hearing: what does the losing choice do well, and when might someone prefer it?
